'Trainee, don't speak to guests unless asked.' We wore grey while staff wore blue. At first I kept a notebook of ideas, like moving the breakfast queue so it didn't block the lift. I'd just started believing I wasn't the kind of person who answers. And underneath, I was angry all the time at everyone in blue. The first time anyone there called me Jahnavi was my last day.

The worst part was I started to believe I wasn't the kind of person who designs. It took a new master, years later, asking for my notebook, to remind me that the apprentice was a role, not me.

Maria, twenty, six weeks into her ground-staff traineeship, stood in her grey trainee vest while the blue-vest staff ran the counters. Trainees were not to speak on the microphone or answer rebooking questions; for six weeks she had been told, "Trainee, move the trolleys," "Trainee, stay back." A mother with a baby asked her which counter handled the Kochi flight. Maria knew. She had studied the board all morning. But she heard herself say, "Sorry, I'm only a trainee, please ask the desk." The mother turned away, tired. Simran, the other trainee, looked at her. "You knew that." Maria shrugged, jaw tight. "What's the point? They don't want us to think." She pushed the next trolley harder than she needed to.

passage: Jomon, you think the new trainees at your office are lazy because they don't speak up? Let me tell you something. I'm Samir chacha, and at nineteen I was a trainee in a big hotel kitchen in Goa. We wore different caps from the chefs. They called us "the caps." We weren't allowed to talk unless asked, eat before the staff, or suggest anything. The first month, I came full of ideas. By the third month, I stopped even thinking of ideas. I kept my head down, did what I was told, and began to believe I was just a pair of hands. When a chef asked my opinion once, I couldn't answer; I'd forgotten I had one. It was only after I left that job that I got my voice back. So be careful, beta. Sometimes people become what they're treated as.

My first year as a trainee in the bank branch taught me something I didn't want to learn. I'm Lakshmi.
The seniors called all trainees "the kids." We made the photocopies, fetched tea, stayed late. Sarita, the senior clerk, never used my name.
At first I was angry. By the fourth month I was something else: quiet. I stopped suggesting things. When a customer asked me a question I knew, I said, "Let me ask a senior."
One day my old college friend visited and said, "You used to be so sharp. What happened?"
I realised I had started to believe I was just "the kid." That scared me.
I'm now in my second year. I still catch myself waiting to be told.

Kalyani

passage: In the tailor's shop in the town of Bhadrachalam, Lakshmi had been 'the helper' for a year. Madhav Anna, the master tailor, never let her cut cloth; she swept threads, ironed and fetched tea. Customers spoke over her head to him. At first she practised cutting on old newspaper at night, dreaming of her own shop. By the monsoon she had stopped. When a customer asked her something about a blouse pattern, she said, 'Ask Anna,' though she knew the answer better than he did. She was starting to believe she was only good for sweeping. One evening her younger sister found the newspaper patterns under the bed. 'These are so good. Why did you stop?' Lakshmi shrugged, then felt a hot flash of resentment, not at her sister, at the whole year. 'Because everyone treats me like the helper,' she said. 'And I started to believe them.'

Then came a flash of anger, at the kitchen and at herself for believing them, and she went to bed without finishing the orange.
